restatements.text: Provides the title of the measure as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Establishes the short title of the Act.
Presents legislative findings and declarations regarding healthcare, education, food assistance, and the wealth of billionaires in California.
States the purpose and intent of the measure to fund public services through a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.

Amends the state constitution to authorize a one-time tax on personal property and wealth of billionaires, creates the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, allocates 90% of revenues to health and 10% to education and food assistance, and exempts these funds from standard state appropriation limits.

Details the specific allowable uses for the Health Account and Education and Food Assistance Account, authorizes the legislature to appropriate up to specific annual limits, provides a start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board, and requires annual reporting by the Department of Finance.
Cites the part as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act within the Revenue and Taxation Code.

Imposes a 5% excise tax for the 2026 tax year on the net worth of applicable individuals and trusts with a net worth of $1 billion or more, and requires resident taxpayers to declare whether their assets exceed this threshold.
Specifies the conditions under which genuine debts and liabilities may reduce a taxpayer's net worth for the purposes of the tax.

Establishes comprehensive rules and methods for determining the fair market value of various asset types, including publicly traded assets, sole proprietorships, business entities, and trusts, while exempting certain retirement accounts and directly held real property.
Allows qualifying liquidity-constrained taxpayers to initiate an Optional Deferral Account (ODA) to defer tax payments on specific assets until those assets are distributed or sold.
Requires appraisers making certified appraisals to send copies to the board and allows the board to impose penalties on appraisers for substantial or gross undervaluation.
Provides rules for apportioning the tax for part-year residents and allows for alternative apportionment methods if the standard method does not fairly represent wealth accumulation in the state.
Allows a pro rata credit against the tax for net wealth taxes paid to other jurisdictions.
Defines key terms used in the administration of the tax, including applicable individual, net worth, valuation date, and tax obligation date.
Grants the Franchise Tax Board authority to adopt regulations to administer the tax and temporarily exempts the board from the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act.
Permits the legislature to amend the Act by a two-thirds vote, provided the amendments further the Act's purposes.
Includes a severability clause and instructs courts to preserve the imposition of the tax to the maximum extent possible if any provision is found invalid.
Establishes financial penalties for substantial or gross understatements of tax and empowers the board to ignore transactions lacking economic substance designed to avoid the tax.
Requires that the provisions of the part be liberally construed to effectuate its purposes.
Authorizes an expedited validation action in Sacramento County Superior Court to determine the facial validity of the Act without requiring prior payment of the tax.
Prohibits taxpayers from deducting the state wealth tax when calculating their state income tax.
Declares that if another measure taxing billionaire net worth appears on the same ballot, this measure shall prevail entirely if it receives more affirmative votes.
Grants the measure's proponent, or any citizen of the state, standing to defend the legality of the Act in court.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. Currently, California does not impose a statewide tax on net worth. The measure enacts a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of applicable individuals with at least $1 billion in wealth, creating a new Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund to allocate the proceeds to health care, public education, and food assistance.

Direct costs include administrative, appraisal, and auditing expenses for the Franchise Tax Board, which is authorized to receive up to a $50 million initial loan for implementation. Taxpayers face substantial compliance costs to appraise complex and illiquid assets. Opportunity costs may include capital flight or reduced investment if high-net-worth individuals leave the state.

The tax is paid by California residents with a net worth over $1 billion. Beneficiaries include low- and moderate-income individuals relying on Medi-Cal and CalFresh, public school students, and the healthcare and education providers that receive the newly appropriated funds.

High-net-worth individuals may relocate their domicile out of California, restructure asset ownership, or place wealth into exempt vehicles. Taxpayers and the state will likely engage in prolonged litigation over valuations of private business entities and the constitutionality of taxing wealth.

The measure asserts that impending federal funding cuts threaten California's healthcare and education safety nets, and that billionaires pay a disproportionately low effective tax rate on their wealth growth. The mechanism is a one-time 5% excise tax on billionaire wealth, bypassing the general fund to dedicate revenues directly to the identified programs.

The Franchise Tax Board gains extensive discretionary power to determine net worth, assess penalties for undervaluation, and define abusive transactions, temporarily exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act. The state legislature gains billions in new earmarked funds to appropriate for specific public programs.

The effect on jobs and investment is disputed. Proponents argue that funding healthcare and education supports a healthier, more educated workforce and prevents harmful cuts to public services. Opponents and some economists argue that a wealth tax discourages entrepreneurship and drives high-net-worth individuals out of the state, reducing capital investment and job creation.

Administration will be highly complex and costly. Valuing illiquid assets like private equity and sole proprietorships is notoriously difficult and subjective. The FTB will likely require extensive outside legal and appraisal expertise, leading to high auditing costs and protracted litigation over valuations and constitutional challenges.

The measure amends both the California Constitution and state statute. The statutory provisions can be amended by the legislature with a two-thirds vote, but only if the changes further the act's purposes. Repealing the tax or changing its core structure would require another statewide ballot measure.

flags.note: Grants the board expansive discretion to redefine or ignore transactions based on ambiguous intent tests.

flags.quote: (c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth
flags.note: Overrides other constitutional provisions regarding property taxation limits.

flags.quote: (h) Notwithstanding Section 32 or any other provision of law, a facial challenge to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act is authorized to be adjudicated through a validation action
flags.note: Overrides standard procedural requirements and constraints for challenging a tax.

flags.quote: (c) ... (8) The Board shall adopt regulations regarding the taxability of receivables and similar assets under this Part.
flags.note: The exact taxation of certain assets depends on future Board regulations.

flags.quote: (a) The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as “the Act,” are severable.
flags.note: Includes a severability clause to preserve the act if parts are struck down.

flags.quote: (a) An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026 on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth by applicable individuals with net worth of $1 billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) or more
flags.note: Specifies the tax applies exclusively to the 2026 tax year.

flags.quote: 50310. Legislative Authority. The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Requires a two-thirds supermajority and limits amendments to those furthering the act's purposes.

flags.quote: Sec. 9. Proponent Standing... the proponent, or in the absence of a proponent, any citizen of this State may defend the legality of this Act... and is authorized to sue directly or intervene for the purpose of defending this Act
flags.note: Creates a private right of action for any citizen to defend the act in court.
